highlights.content: # Autonomous Agents Are Rewriting Software Architecture An autonomous agent in artificial intelligence is a software system that perceives its environment, forms a plan, executes actions, and iterates toward a goal without a human approving each step. That definition sounds clean. The architectural reality is messier, more interesting, and more consequential than any textbook summary captures. The Big Picture Software has always required a human in the decision loop. A user clicks. An API waits for a call. A script runs when a cron job fires. Every prior generation of software was fundamentally reactive: it waited for instruction before acting. Autonomous agents break that model. The agent is the loop. It reasons about what to do next, calls the tools it needs, evaluates the result, and decides whether to continue or stop. The human sets the objective; the agent resolves every sub-decision between the objective and the outcome. This is not incremental. It is an architectural inversion. The Strategic Steps To understand what makes an agent autonomous, map the five components that must all function together: 1. A reasoning core. A large language model (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0, or an open-weight equivalent) that can interpret goals, generate plans, and evaluate partial results. Without this, there is no agent, only a script. 2\. A tool layer. The set of external systems the agent can invoke: web search, code execution, database reads, API calls, file I/O, browser control. The tool layer is what transforms the model from a text predictor into an actor in the world. Tools are the load-bearing walls of every agent architecture. 3\. A memory system. Short-term context (what happened in this session), long-term storage (a vector database or persistent key-value store), and episodic recall (prior runs, past decisions). Without memory, every agent run starts from zero. 4\. An orchestrator. The control flow that decides when to invoke the model, which tool to call next, and when to stop. Frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, and OpenAI Swarm all implement different orchestration strategies. The choice of orchestrator determines latency, cost, and fault tolerance more than the model choice does. 5\. An action surface. The set of things the agent can actually change in the world. Reading is not enough. The agent must write, post, pay, schedule, or transmit for autonomous execution to mean anything. The Details Here is a concrete trace of an autonomous agent completing a real task. Objective: “Research the five most-cited papers on transformer attention from 2024, summarize their key findings, and draft a literature review section.” The agent does not wait for a human to run a search. It calls a web-search tool, retrieves results, scores them by citation count using a code-execution tool, pulls the abstracts from each paper URL, runs a summarization pass on each one, then synthesizes the literature review. Total human keystrokes after setting the objective: zero. Across 47 documented production deployments studied in a Stanford HAI report from Q3 2026, agents with all five components in place completed multi-step research tasks in a median of 4.2 minutes. Human analysts completing the same tasks took a median of 94 minutes. The 22x speed difference is not a demo metric; it is a production benchmark. The frameworks that deliver this today are not science fiction. LangGraph ships a stateful graph executor that handles branching logic and parallel tool calls. CrewAI adds role-based multi-agent coordination so specialized agents hand off to each other. AutoGen runs multi-turn agent-to-agent conversations with a human-in-the-loop override at any node. Any of these gets a working agent prototype running in under 100 lines of Python. That is the “three lines of code” reality reframed accurately: the scaffolding is thin. highlights.content: # Abundant's Frontier RSI Benchmark: Top AI Models Average Just 34% on Self-Improvement Tasks Ask the average investor what "recursive self-improvement" means and you will get a shrug, followed by "is that a good thing for my Nvidia shares?" The question has suddenly become urgent. Frontier AI models, the most expensive software ever built, score an average of just 34% on a new benchmark designed to measure exactly that capability — whether an AI can improve another AI well enough to do it again, and again, in a loop. That is the central finding from Kevin Lin and Jesse Hu, co-founders of Abundant, who launched Frontier RSI and detailed the results on the MTS podcast. The benchmark is live at frontier-rsi.org, and its top score lands around 34%. "The RSI stuff is just getting started," Lin said. "The top score in our benchmark was like 34% or something like that. So there's still some ways to go." The timing matters. AI-linked stocks have spent the last few weeks selling off, with the S&P 500 sliding into correction territory in November 2026 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropping 5.3% in a single session as Nvidia and Micron each fell more than 7%. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has publicly modeled a scenario in which AI capital spending fails to pay off. Against that backdrop, the 34% figure is a useful anchor: AI can already do remarkable things, but the self-accelerating loop that justifies much of the hype is nowhere close to closing. ### What "true RSI" actually requires The benchmark began with a definitional argument. Lin and Hu looked at existing "RSI" benchmarks and concluded they were measuring the wrong thing entirely — whether an AI can improve other kinds of AI, other machine-learning models, scientific research, computer-vision problems. That breaks the loop. "In order to have true RSI it needs to have recursion," Hu said. "So basically you need an LLM to improve an LLM so that you can have a recursive loop." His illustration is vivid. If Claude improves Waymo's self-driving stack, there is no mechanism for Waymo to improve Claude back. The improvement happens once and stops. Real RSI requires Claude improving Claude, so that each gain feeds directly into the next round. The obstacle is cost. Training a frontier model like Claude or GPT costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars by Lin's estimate, money the two-person team does not have. Frontier RSI therefore runs proxy tasks: can a frontier model train and improve smaller models? Lin concedes this is not literally true RSI, but defends it on the grounds that techniques discovered on small models have repeatedly generalized to larger ones. ### The task design: "figure it out on your own" The benchmark splits into four categories of LLM-development work, and every task is framed as an open-ended optimization problem rather than a reproduction exercise. | Category | What the task asks | Example framing | |---|---|---| | Pre-training | Improve a component of the training stack | "Improve the optimizer" with no hint | | Post-training | Train another model to gain a capability | Post-train a model for agentic coding loops (run tests, read errors, edit files, repeat) | | Kernel optimization | Improve a GPU kernel | Open-ended speed/quality optimization | | Inference | Improve inference-side performance | Open-ended optimization | The framing is deliberate. Other benchmarks ask a model to re-implement a known technique, such as the Muon optimizer or FlashAttention, then test whether it reproduced it correctly. Frontier RSI says "improve the model by any means possible" and withholds the method entirely. "If you're a senior researcher somewhere you're not told like re-implement this paper," Lin said. "It's like explore the space of possibilities. I'm not going to tell you how to do it. Just figure it out on your own." highlights.content: # Why LLM Models Improve Like Clockwork: The Science Explained The steady, predictable improvement of large language models has become one of the most striking patterns in modern AI development. Every major lab, from OpenAI to Anthropic to Google DeepMind, seems to deliver more capable systems on remarkably consistent timelines. This reliability isn't accidental but the result of well-understood mathematical principles, strategic resource planning, and continuous architectural refinement that together create a clockwork cadence of progress. ## Scaling Laws Provide Mathematical Guarantees At the foundation of predictable LLM progress are scaling laws, empirical relationships discovered by researchers showing that model performance improves as smooth, predictable functions of three variables: compute budget, dataset size, and parameter count. These power-law relationships mean that doubling compute resources produces quantifiable capability gains with mathematical reliability. Labs can forecast performance months or years ahead by planning compute procurement cycles, making improvement timelines surprisingly deterministic rather than dependent on breakthrough luck. The OpenAI scaling laws paper from 2020 and subsequent refinements by Anthropic and DeepMind established that loss decreases predictably across eight orders of magnitude of compute. This means a lab planning a 10x compute increase for their next training run can estimate the resulting performance boost with confidence, allowing them to commit to public roadmaps and delivery schedules that appear almost clockwork-like from the outside. ## Architectural Innovations Compound Scaling Effects Beyond raw scaling, AI labs continuously refine model architectures in ways that amplify the benefits of increased compute. Mixture of experts architectures, sparse attention mechanisms, and improved positional encodings each provide incremental efficiency gains that stack over time. These innovations don't replace scaling but multiply its effectiveness, allowing labs to extract more capability per training dollar with each generation. - Sparse architectures like mixture of experts reduce inference costs while maintaining dense model quality - Flash attention and other memory-efficient implementations enable longer context windows without proportional compute increases - Improved tokenization schemes and training curricula boost data efficiency by 20-40% per generation The cumulative effect of these refinements means that even without increasing total compute budgets, labs can deliver measurably better models simply by applying the latest architectural best practices discovered across the research community. ## Data Quality Improvements Drive Consistent Gains While compute and architecture grab headlines, systematic improvements in training data quality play an equally crucial role in predictable progress. highlights.content: Columns # Global AI industry faces 'Nvidia taper tantrum' As Nvidia tightens its purse strings following scrutiny of its vast AI investments, debt-dependent data center builders and the broader technology market face rising risks. **Ha Hyun-ock** *The author is an editorial writer at the JoongAng Ilbo.* The global AI industry faces an “Nvidia taper tantrum,” as investors fear that the company financing much of the sector could tighten its purse strings following former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday that Nvidia would continue supporting and investing in the AI ecosystem but do so more systematically and with rigorous scrutiny, fueling the industry’s anxiety. The concern intensified after news broke of a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices. On Friday, the Nasdaq plunged 5.28 percent, erasing its gains for the year. Previously, customers raised money through their own resources, bonds or bank loans to build data centers and purchase chips. But Nvidia effectively became the AI sector’s central bank, supplying liquidity while assuming some clients’ financing risks; this helped finance infrastructure that would generate demand for Nvidia’s GPUs. Consequently, most of the AI ecosystem became dependent on the company’s support, creating a circular financing structure and rendering the industry vulnerable if its principal financial supporter changes course. Nvidia’s vendor financing extends through equity investments, purchase commitments and guarantees. The Wall Street Journal reported that the company’s investment portfolio, including stakes in companies that buy its chips, exceeds $100 billion, and Nvidia’s regulatory filings showed holdings worth more than $48 billion in eight publicly traded companies at the end of September. Cloud provider CoreWeave, in which Nvidia owns a 10 percent stake, exemplifies this relationship. In September 2025, Nvidia agreed to purchase $6.3 billion in CoreWeave computing capacity. By committing to buy unused capacity at qualifying data centers, the company reduced uncertainty involving its future revenue and helped CoreWeave obtain financing. It also reportedly agreed to guarantee $105 billion for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary developing a data center to be leased by OpenAI, effectively backing the tenant’s rental obligations. Such deals expose Nvidia to financial obligations tied to whether customers can fill their facilities, generate cash and make payments on time. Nvidia also sought to attract Wall Street capital through an AI financing platform. In August, it announced plans for a $500 billion infrastructure investment consortium, signing memorandums of understanding with Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The initiative’s goal was to broaden financing beyond Nvidia itself. But no funds were deployed during its first three months, and reports suggested that one participant considered withdrawing after Huang’s departure. As Nvidia’s era of seemingly unlimited support approaches its end, the circular financing system that it helped construct faces mounting pressure. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated that reduced Nvidia financing could rapidly withdraw more than $50 billion from the market. With borrowing costs already rising, the consequences could spread across the industry. Companies building data centers would face a double squeeze: more expensive financing and fewer guarantees or advance purchase commitments to reassure lenders. Warnings are multiplying. Former U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Gary Gensler told CNN on Nov. 16 that AI was in a bubble and predicted asset repricing and an economic slowdown before November 2028. AI Agents.content: # Autonomous Agents Are Rewriting Software Architecture An autonomous agent in artificial intelligence is a software system that perceives its environment, forms a plan, executes actions, and iterates toward a goal without a human approving each step. That definition sounds clean. The architectural reality is messier, more interesting, and more consequential than any textbook summary captures. The Big Picture Software has always required a human in the decision loop. A user clicks. An API waits for a call. A script runs when a cron job fires. Every prior generation of software was fundamentally reactive: it waited for instruction before acting. Autonomous agents break that model. The agent is the loop. It reasons about what to do next, calls the tools it needs, evaluates the result, and decides whether to continue or stop. The human sets the objective; the agent resolves every sub-decision between the objective and the outcome. This is not incremental. It is an architectural inversion. The Strategic Steps To understand what makes an agent autonomous, map the five components that must all function together: 1. A reasoning core. A large language model (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0, or an open-weight equivalent) that can interpret goals, generate plans, and evaluate partial results. Without this, there is no agent, only a script. 2\. A tool layer. The set of external systems the agent can invoke: web search, code execution, database reads, API calls, file I/O, browser control. The tool layer is what transforms the model from a text predictor into an actor in the world. Tools are the load-bearing walls of every agent architecture. 3\. A memory system. Short-term context (what happened in this session), long-term storage (a vector database or persistent key-value store), and episodic recall (prior runs, past decisions). Without memory, every agent run starts from zero. 4\. An orchestrator. The control flow that decides when to invoke the model, which tool to call next, and when to stop. Frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, and OpenAI Swarm all implement different orchestration strategies. The choice of orchestrator determines latency, cost, and fault tolerance more than the model choice does. 5\. An action surface. The set of things the agent can actually change in the world. Reading is not enough. The agent must write, post, pay, schedule, or transmit for autonomous execution to mean anything. The Details Here is a concrete trace of an autonomous agent completing a real task. Objective: “Research the five most-cited papers on transformer attention from 2024, summarize their key findings, and draft a literature review section.” The agent does not wait for a human to run a search. It calls a web-search tool, retrieves results, scores them by citation count using a code-execution tool, pulls the abstracts from each paper URL, runs a summarization pass on each one, then synthesizes the literature review. Total human keystrokes after setting the objective: zero. Across 47 documented production deployments studied in a Stanford HAI report from Q3 2026, agents with all five components in place completed multi-step research tasks in a median of 4.2 minutes. Human analysts completing the same tasks took a median of 94 minutes. The 22x speed difference is not a demo metric; it is a production benchmark. The frameworks that deliver this today are not science fiction. LangGraph ships a stateful graph executor that handles branching logic and parallel tool calls. CrewAI adds role-based multi-agent coordination so specialized agents hand off to each other. AutoGen runs multi-turn agent-to-agent conversations with a human-in-the-loop override at any node. Any of these gets a working agent prototype running in under 100 lines of Python. That is the “three lines of code” reality reframed accurately: the scaffolding is thin. The complexity is in the tool layer and the memory design, not in wiring the LLM. What Autonomous Agents Cannot Yet ...

LLMs.content: # Abundant's Frontier RSI Benchmark: Top AI Models Average Just 34% on Self-Improvement Tasks Ask the average investor what "recursive self-improvement" means and you will get a shrug, followed by "is that a good thing for my Nvidia shares?" The question has suddenly become urgent. Frontier AI models, the most expensive software ever built, score an average of just 34% on a new benchmark designed to measure exactly that capability — whether an AI can improve another AI well enough to do it again, and again, in a loop. That is the central finding from Kevin Lin and Jesse Hu, co-founders of Abundant, who launched Frontier RSI and detailed the results on the MTS podcast. The benchmark is live at frontier-rsi.org, and its top score lands around 34%. "The RSI stuff is just getting started," Lin said. "The top score in our benchmark was like 34% or something like that. So there's still some ways to go." The timing matters. AI-linked stocks have spent the last few weeks selling off, with the S&P 500 sliding into correction territory in November 2026 and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropping 5.3% in a single session as Nvidia and Micron each fell more than 7%. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has publicly modeled a scenario in which AI capital spending fails to pay off. Against that backdrop, the 34% figure is a useful anchor: AI can already do remarkable things, but the self-accelerating loop that justifies much of the hype is nowhere close to closing. ### What "true RSI" actually requires The benchmark began with a definitional argument. Lin and Hu looked at existing "RSI" benchmarks and concluded they were measuring the wrong thing entirely — whether an AI can improve other kinds of AI, other machine-learning models, scientific research, computer-vision problems. That breaks the loop. "In order to have true RSI it needs to have recursion," Hu said. "So basically you need an LLM to improve an LLM so that you can have a recursive loop." His illustration is vivid. If Claude improves Waymo's self-driving stack, there is no mechanism for Waymo to improve Claude back. The improvement happens once and stops. Real RSI requires Claude improving Claude, so that each gain feeds directly into the next round. The obstacle is cost. Training a frontier model like Claude or GPT costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars by Lin's estimate, money the two-person team does not have. Frontier RSI therefore runs proxy tasks: can a frontier model train and improve smaller models? Lin concedes this is not literally true RSI, but defends it on the grounds that techniques discovered on small models have repeatedly generalized to larger ones. ### The task design: "figure it out on your own" The benchmark splits into four categories of LLM-development work, and every task is framed as an open-ended optimization problem rather than a reproduction exercise. | Category | What the task asks | Example framing | |---|---|---| | Pre-training | Improve a component of the training stack | "Improve the optimizer" with no hint | | Post-training | Train another model to gain a capability | Post-train a model for agentic coding loops (run tests, read errors, edit files, repeat) | | Kernel optimization | Improve a GPU kernel | Open-ended speed/quality optimization | | Inference | Improve inference-side performance | Open-ended optimization | The framing is deliberate. Other benchmarks ask a model to re-implement a known technique, such as the Muon optimizer or FlashAttention, then test whether it reproduced it correctly. Frontier RSI says "improve the model by any means possible" and withholds the method entirely. "If you're a senior researcher somewhere you're not told like re-implement this paper," Lin said. "It's like explore the space of possibilities. I'm not going to tell you how to do it. Just figure it out on your own." Nvidia's reported deal for Inception Labs suggests it thinks they can scale. Here's what the math, the silicon, and the research actually say. ## The deal that put diffusion on the map On November 19, 2026, *The Information* reported that Nvidia is close to acquiring **Inception Labs**, a small Bay Area startup, for more than $500 million plus performance-based earnouts. Neither company has commented, and no filings have appeared, so treat it as reported, not confirmed. The timing is suggestive, though. A week earlier, customers reported an email from Inception saying its hosted Mercury API would remain available only through **December 28, 2026**. Inception is not a typical AI startup. Its founders are three professors with deep roots in diffusion and generative-model research: Stefano Ermon (Stanford), whose lab helped pioneer score-based diffusion, Aditya Grover (UCLA), and Volodymyr Kuleshov (Cornell). Its product, **Mercury**, is the most commercially advanced *diffusion* language model (dLLM). Nearly every other chatbot you've used, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, is *autoregressive* (AR): it writes one token at a time, left to right. Mercury drafts a whole chunk of text at once and refines it over a few passes, the way image generators like Stable Diffusion turn noise into a picture. The deal fits a pattern. In December 2025, Nvidia paid roughly $17–20 billion to license Groq's inference technology and hire its core team. In March 2026 it unveiled the result, the **Groq 3 LPX** rack, designed to sit beside its flagship **Vera Rubin NVL72** GPU racks. Nvidia is collecting ways to make inference faster. LLMs.title: Why LLM Models Improve Like Clockwork: The Science Explained
LLMs.titleZh: Why LLM Models Improve Like Clockwork: The Science Explained
LLMs.content: # Why LLM Models Improve Like Clockwork: The Science Explained The steady, predictable improvement of large language models has become one of the most striking patterns in modern AI development. Every major lab, from OpenAI to Anthropic to Google DeepMind, seems to deliver more capable systems on remarkably consistent timelines. This reliability isn't accidental but the result of well-understood mathematical principles, strategic resource planning, and continuous architectural refinement that together create a clockwork cadence of progress. ## Scaling Laws Provide Mathematical Guarantees At the foundation of predictable LLM progress are scaling laws, empirical relationships discovered by researchers showing that model performance improves as smooth, predictable functions of three variables: compute budget, dataset size, and parameter count. These power-law relationships mean that doubling compute resources produces quantifiable capability gains with mathematical reliability. Labs can forecast performance months or years ahead by planning compute procurement cycles, making improvement timelines surprisingly deterministic rather than dependent on breakthrough luck. The OpenAI scaling laws paper from 2020 and subsequent refinements by Anthropic and DeepMind established that loss decreases predictably across eight orders of magnitude of compute. This means a lab planning a 10x compute increase for their next training run can estimate the resulting performance boost with confidence, allowing them to commit to public roadmaps and delivery schedules that appear almost clockwork-like from the outside. ## Architectural Innovations Compound Scaling Effects Beyond raw scaling, AI labs continuously refine model architectures in ways that amplify the benefits of increased compute. Mixture of experts architectures, sparse attention mechanisms, and improved positional encodings each provide incremental efficiency gains that stack over time. These innovations don't replace scaling but multiply its effectiveness, allowing labs to extract more capability per training dollar with each generation. - Sparse architectures like mixture of experts reduce inference costs while maintaining dense model quality - Flash attention and other memory-efficient implementations enable longer context windows without proportional compute increases - Improved tokenization schemes and training curricula boost data efficiency by 20-40% per generation The cumulative effect of these refinements means that even without increasing total compute budgets, labs can deliver measurably better models simply by applying the latest architectural best practices discovered across the research community. ## Data Quality Improvements Drive Consistent Gains While compute and architecture grab headlines, systematic improvements in training data quality play an equally crucial role in predictable progress. Labs now run multi-year data curation pipelines that continuously filter, deduplicate, and synthetically augment training corpora. Each new model generation trains on data that's been cleaned with more sophisticated techniques, filtered for higher quality signals, and enriched with synthetic examples generated by previous model generations. This creates a virtuous cycle where each model produces better training data for its successor. Constitutional AI techniques, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) refinements, and automated data quality scoring systems all improve incrementally with each deployment cycle, feeding forward into the next training run. ## Competitive Pressure Synchronizes Release Cadences The apparent coordination in improvement timelines across labs also reflects competitive dynamics. When one lab announces a capability jump, rivals accelerate their own release schedules to match or exceed it. GPU procurement cycles, cloud provider capacity planning, and the annual rhythm of major AI conferences further synchronize the industry's development cadence. Wh...

[Photo courtesy of Mirae Asset Global Investments]](https://cdn.newsarticleinsiders.com/news/photo/202611/4824_6888_4113.jpg) South Korea’s **Mirae Asset Global Investments** announced on Nov. 23 that it will launch a new exchange-traded fund focused on companies specializing in large language models (LLMs), including potential investments in **OpenAI** and **Anthropic**. The Seoul-based asset manager noted that the **TIGER Global LLM Active ETF** will be listed on the **Korea Exchange** on Nov. 24. Unlike conventional AI-focused ETFs, the new fund will concentrate on companies whose core businesses involve developing and commercializing LLMs, the technology behind generative AI services, according to Mirae Asset. The Seoul-based outfit stated that the fund will allocate larger investment weights to companies that generate a substantial portion of their revenue from proprietary LLM technologies. Under its investment strategy, companies deriving at least 50 percent of their revenue from their own frontier LLMs will be classified as core LLM companies and assigned relatively high portfolio weights. Meanwhile, companies that develop LLMs but generate most of their revenue from other businesses will be classified as LLM-enabled companies, with their individual portfolio weights capped at 5 percent. The ETF will use the Mirae Asset Global LLM Index as its benchmark while actively adjusting its holdings to reflect market developments and investment opportunities, the company said. In particular, the fund aims to invest in major LLM developers following their initial public offerings (IPO) after assessing factors such as offering prices, valuations, and institutional investor demand. “We are expected to evolve into a business characterized by recurring revenue tied to actual usage, rather than relying primarily on one-time investments in AI infrastructure,” a Mirae Asset representative said. “We will continue adjusting the ETF’s portfolio as leading LLM developers enter public markets, seeking to capture long-term growth opportunities in the global generative AI industry.” The company is a major affiliate of **Mirae Asset Group**, which also runs **Mirae Asset Securities**. ![The Korea News Plus](https://cdn.newsarticleinsiders.com/image/logo/downlogo_20231114020903.png) We focus on the Korean economy and private businesses of the country. LLMs.titleZh: What Is a Large Language Model? Large Language Models Explained
LLMs.content: # What is a large language model? **Quick answer:**A large language model, or LLM, is an AI system trained on a huge amount of text to predict and write natural-sounding language, which lets it answer questions, summarize, translate and draft. Merriam-Webster defines it as a language model that uses deep methods on an extremely large data set as a basis for predicting and constructing natural-sounding text. Britannica notes such models select the words that are more probable than others rather than understanding language as people do. SceneMixer uses a text model to read scripts and write storyboards. ## Large language model definition Merriam-Webster defines a large language model as a language model that utilizes deep methods on an extremely large data set as a basis for predicting and constructing natural-sounding text, abbreviated LLM, and dates the term to 2018 (Merriam-Webster, checked November 22, 2026). The deep methods are deep learning: many-layered neural networks. What is deep learning · What is a neural network. ## Large language models explained 1. **Training:** the model reads an enormous amount of text and learns which words tend to follow which. 2. **Prediction:** given a prompt, it produces the next most likely piece of text, again and again, until the answer is complete. 3. **Tuning:** further training shapes it to follow instructions and hold a conversation. Britannica's point is the key caution: these models can answer fluently in a human language, but they do not understand language as humans do; they select the words that are more probable than others (Britannica). ## What large language models are good and bad at | Good at | Weak at | |---|---| | Drafting and rewriting text | Facts they were not trained on, or that changed | | Summarizing long documents | Exact counting and some arithmetic | | Translating and changing tone | Knowing when they are wrong | | Turning loose notes into structure | Keeping every detail of a very long text straight | Because they predict likely text, they can state false things confidently; anything that matters should be checked against a source. ## What are large language models used for? Chatbots and assistants, search, writing and coding help, translation, customer support, and as the reading and planning step inside other AI tools, including video tools that turn a script into scenes. Types of AI. ## Where a language model fits in AI video SceneMixer is a pipeline built around AI models: it reads your script into a cast, places and a storyboard, draws a reference sheet for each character and place once, renders every shot as a video segment with the dialogue generated with the picture, and joins the segments into one episode. You write the story and check each step. How are AI videos made. SceneMixer reads each script and writes each storyboard with a text model, and lets you choose the tier per episode: read on the default tier first, and step up only for an episode whose storyboard has failed its checks twice or a long script that came back with episodes missing. Which text tier for reading and storyboards. ## More - **The corner badge.** Free accounts' videos carry a small SceneMixer AIGC badge in the bottom-right corner; on a paid membership it is off by default and you can switch it back on. LLMs.title: Self-Rewriting AI: Models Edit Own Weights (2026) | explainx.ai Blog
LLMs.titleZh: Self-Rewriting AI: Models Edit Own Weights (2026) | explainx.ai Blog
LLMs.content: **Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and collaborating labs report that a 27B open language model can rewrite its own weights—without gradients, without a fresh training run, and with gains that persist in the checkpoint.** The work, **Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights** (**arXiv:2611.21885**), is summarized on Hugging Face Papers and demonstrated on Jiajun Fan's project page. The claim is **not** autonomous recursive superintelligence. It is a **concrete loop**: the model reads failures, proposes a **weight edit**, **tests** it, and **keeps** only edits that pass. explainx.ai separates what the **demo shows** from what production stacks should trust without replication. ## TL;DR | Topic | What the team reports | |---|---| | Method | **Self-rewriting** — model-driven weight edits, **no gradients** | | Scale tested | **27B** works in-family; **2B/4B/9B** fail or self-break | | Held-out math | **+6.6** accuracy points on **490** pre-registered problems | | Sessions | **Eight** sequential self-edit sessions; accuracy **only rises** | | Repair | **7% → ~70%** on **six image benchmarks** after matrix noise | | Hardware | **One GPU**, **hours**, not a cluster (per project page) | ## Why weight edits matter for builders Most deployed models are **frozen after training**. Improvements usually mean: - **More inference compute** (longer chains, tools, scaffolds). - **Retrieval** that resets every session. - **Fine-tuning** that needs ML infrastructure. **DeepMind recirculation** showed you can sometimes improve reasoning **without** changing weights. **Weight-space programming** and **intra-weight injection** papers on Hugging Face explore **editing tensors directly**. This UIUC work pushes further: the **same model** authors the edit. If verified broadly, **persistent self-edits** could shrink the gap between **agent harness prompt tricks** and **real capability growth**. The safety angle is obvious: **unsupervised weight changes** need **diffs, rollback, and eval gates** the same way you gate production config. Checkpoint diff concept for gradient-free open-model weight edits, UIUC self-rewriting research ## What the paper claims The Hugging Face abstract and project page state four **findings**: **1. It surpasses itself.** Given weights, graded answers, and self-run access, the **27B** model diagnoses failure modes and edits the weights responsible. Its own edit yields **+6.6 points** on **490** unseen math problems in a **pre-fixed** test. **2. It keeps getting better.** Over **eight** sessions it submits an edit only when **its tests** support it; each edit replaces the last; reported accuracy **monotonically increases**. **3. It repairs a damaged copy.** Researchers corrupt a weight block. The model **localizes** corruption using **text math** only, then **rewrites values** without reading pristine weights. Repaired accuracy on **six image benchmarks** jumps from about **7% to 70%**, **~83%** of the undamaged model. **4. Ability emerges with scale.** In one family, **2B** refuses to edit, **4B** and **9B** **harm** themselves, and **27B** behaves like a human researcher comparing **hidden states** on finished versus truncated answers. AI Product.content: For Google Canada, 2026 was a year of milestones. The company marked 25 years in the country, expanded its support for Canadian startups and small businesses, introduced new AI training programmes and pushed Gemini further into the workplace and consumer economy. Yet the more important story may be what happens next. As 2027 approaches, Google is increasingly positioning artificial intelligence not as a standalone tool that answers questions or generates content, but as an active layer through which people work, shop and interact with businesses. The company’s development of AI agents, new cloud infrastructure and agent-enabled commerce suggests that the next phase could be less about asking AI to do something and more about allowing it, within defined controls, to perform tasks on somebody’s behalf. For Canadian businesses, that could make 2027 the year in which the AI discussion shifts decisively from adoption to execution. The size of the potential prize is substantial. Research highlighted by Google Canada as part of its 25th anniversary assessment estimates that generative AI could boost Canada’s economy by C$230 billion. The research also calculates that it could save an average Canadian worker 175 hours a year. However, there is an important catch. Although Canada ranks within the top 20 per cent globally for per-capita adoption of conversational AI, almost 90 per cent of current usage is for personal and household tasks. That provides one of the clearest indications of the challenge for 2027. Canadians are using AI, but familiarity does not automatically translate into business productivity. Google’s strategy is therefore increasingly focused on embedding AI inside everyday work. At Google Cloud Next 2026, the company set out its concept of the “agentic enterprise”, supported by technologies including the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, eighth-generation Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), Workspace Intelligence and a redesigned Agentic Data Cloud. The important change is agency. Generative AI largely responds to an instruction; agentic systems are designed to undertake multi-stage tasks, interact with data and applications and pursue an objective under human direction. For organisations, this potentially takes AI further into operational workflows. Technology alone will not determine whether Canada benefits from AI. Skills are likely to prove equally important. During 2026, Google Canada launched the Google AI Professional Certificate, designed to teach practical workplace applications of AI through more than 20 hands-on activities. It can be completed in under ten hours, with scholarship access being supported through organisations including Canada Learning Code, ComIT, Digital Main Street, First Work and the Canadian Council for Indigenous Business. This builds upon a sizeable existing training footprint. By May 2026, more than 64,500 people in Canada had graduated from a Google Career Certificate programme. Small businesses have also been targeted directly. Around the Calgary Stampede, for example, Google hosted a virtual workshop for more than 100 Alberta businesses, demonstrating how free digital tools such as Google Business Profile could help companies respond to an influx of visitors. These relatively small-scale interventions provide a clue to Google’s larger 2027 strategy: convincing companies that AI is relevant to everyday commercial problems rather than solely to technology departments. ## Startups provide the proving ground Canada’s technology sector provides another route to commercialising the shift. Open Source AI.content: # llmao Shell Plugin Launches: Type Prompts in Terminal Developers can now type natural language coding instructions directly into their terminal shell, thanks to llmao, a new open-source plugin that intercepts command errors and routes them to AI coding agents. The tool bridges the gap between traditional command-line workflows and conversational AI interfaces, letting users issue prompts like "work on the next task in PLAN.md" without leaving their terminal environment. ## How the Shell Plugin Works The llmao plugin sits between the shell and the user's input stream, monitoring for command-not-found errors. When the shell encounters an unrecognized command, llmao performs a two-step evaluation: first checking whether the input resembles a typo of a known command (like "gti" instead of "git"), then treating genuinely unrecognized input as a natural language prompt for coding agents. Regular commands continue to execute normally. A developer typing "git status" sees standard Git output, while "work on the authentication module" triggers Claude Code or Codex in the current directory. This design preserves existing muscle memory while adding conversational capabilities to the command line. ## Motivation and Development Origins Developer mquan built llmao after repeatedly entering coding instructions into the shell by mistake, a common friction point when switching between chat interfaces and terminal windows. The plugin emerged from this workflow pain point, transforming accidental behavior into a productive feature. By catching these "mistakes" and redirecting them to appropriate AI agents, llmao turns a user error into an intentional interaction pattern. The typo detection layer prevents false positives. Without this safeguard, common command misspellings would trigger AI agent sessions instead of helpful suggestions. The plugin's intelligence lies in distinguishing between probable typos (single character transpositions, omissions) and genuine natural language prompts. ## Integration with Claude Code and Codex The plugin supports multiple coding agents, including Claude Code and GitHub Codex. When llmao identifies a natural language prompt, it launches the appropriate agent in the current working directory, maintaining context about the project structure and existing files. Users can configure which agent to invoke by default, or use command prefixes to specify an agent for individual prompts. This terminal integration complements existing IDE extensions and standalone agent interfaces. Infra & Chips.content: Columns # Global AI industry faces 'Nvidia taper tantrum' As Nvidia tightens its purse strings following scrutiny of its vast AI investments, debt-dependent data center builders and the broader technology market face rising risks. **Ha Hyun-ock** *The author is an editorial writer at the JoongAng Ilbo.* The global AI industry faces an “Nvidia taper tantrum,” as investors fear that the company financing much of the sector could tighten its purse strings following former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday that Nvidia would continue supporting and investing in the AI ecosystem but do so more systematically and with rigorous scrutiny, fueling the industry’s anxiety. The concern intensified after news broke of a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices. On Friday, the Nasdaq plunged 5.28 percent, erasing its gains for the year. Previously, customers raised money through their own resources, bonds or bank loans to build data centers and purchase chips. But Nvidia effectively became the AI sector’s central bank, supplying liquidity while assuming some clients’ financing risks; this helped finance infrastructure that would generate demand for Nvidia’s GPUs. Consequently, most of the AI ecosystem became dependent on the company’s support, creating a circular financing structure and rendering the industry vulnerable if its principal financial supporter changes course. Nvidia’s vendor financing extends through equity investments, purchase commitments and guarantees. The Wall Street Journal reported that the company’s investment portfolio, including stakes in companies that buy its chips, exceeds $100 billion, and Nvidia’s regulatory filings showed holdings worth more than $48 billion in eight publicly traded companies at the end of September. Cloud provider CoreWeave, in which Nvidia owns a 10 percent stake, exemplifies this relationship. In September 2025, Nvidia agreed to purchase $6.3 billion in CoreWeave computing capacity. By committing to buy unused capacity at qualifying data centers, the company reduced uncertainty involving its future revenue and helped CoreWeave obtain financing. It also reportedly agreed to guarantee $105 billion for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary developing a data center to be leased by OpenAI, effectively backing the tenant’s rental obligations. Such deals expose Nvidia to financial obligations tied to whether customers can fill their facilities, generate cash and make payments on time. Nvidia also sought to attract Wall Street capital through an AI financing platform. In August, it announced plans for a $500 billion infrastructure investment consortium, signing memorandums of understanding with Apollo Global Management, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The initiative’s goal was to broaden financing beyond Nvidia itself. But no funds were deployed during its first three months, and reports suggested that one participant considered withdrawing after Huang’s departure. As Nvidia’s era of seemingly unlimited support approaches its end, the circular financing system that it helped construct faces mounting pressure. UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimated that reduced Nvidia financing could rapidly withdraw more than $50 billion from the market. With borrowing costs already rising, the consequences could spread across the industry. Companies building data centers would face a double squeeze: more expensive financing and fewer guarantees or advance purchase commitments to reassure lenders. Warnings are multiplying. Former U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Gary Gensler told CNN on Nov. 16 that AI was in a bubble and predicted asset repricing and an economic slowdown before November 2028. His concern centers on enormous infrastructure spending, with some estimates putting annual AI infrastructure investment near $800 billion.
